claims.text: Increasing local short-range chemical order in single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys increases high-temperature yield strength.
Increasing local short-range chemical order in single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys reduces thermal expansion.
Near-equimolar TaNbHfZr can form a BCC random-solid-solution starting structure.
Homogenization above 1200 K minimizes secondary phases and produces a nominally random TaNbHfZr solid solution.
Minor dopants or changes in elemental ratios can systematically encourage or suppress short-range order.
Short-range chemical order modifies local bonding and the interaction energies experienced by dislocations.
Enhanced short-range order reduces local compositional fluctuations.
Enhanced short-range order increases lattice friction stress.
Enhanced short-range order restricts dislocation glide and slows defect motion.
The dislocation-hindering effect of short-range order causes higher high-temperature yield strength than in a more random solid solution.
The altered local elastic behavior associated with short-range order causes lower thermal expansion.
More strongly ordered alloys may have yield strengths tens of percent higher than the baseline.
More strongly ordered alloys will have a marginally lower thermal expansion coefficient than the baseline.
Short-range order can be detected using diffraction, neutron scattering, and atom-probe-based characterization.
Homogenization or compositional balancing can produce a reference alloy with minimal short-range order that approximates a random solid solution.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to single-phase BCC refractory HEAs tested up to approximately 1300 K.
Intermetallic precipitation or multiphase transformations can alter the role of short-range order at higher temperatures or in other alloy systems.
In TaNbHfZr, yield strength, ductility, local nanostructure, and chemical ordering depend on annealing treatment.

contradictions.description: The intervention says homogenization temperature and cooling rate will be held constant while order is varied compositionally, but the baseline is to be obtained by optimizing homogenization and the falsification design varies thermal histories. These are incompatible definitions of the controlled comparison and introduce processing-history confounding.
